'''Lipót''', or '''Leopold''' (in German), '''Klug''' (23 January 1854 – 24 March 1945) was a [[Jewish-Hungarian]]<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Klug|title=Leopold Klug}}</ref> [[mathematician]], professor in the [[Franz Joseph University]] of [[Kolozsvár]].

== Life and work ==
Klug attended the ''gymnasium'' of his hometown and entered [[Eötvös Loránd University]] in 1872 where he graduated as docent in 1874.{{sfn | Szenkovits | 2014 | p=425 }} Between 1874 and 1893 he taught mathematics in the high school of Pozsony (now [[Bratislava]] in [[Slovakia]]). From 1893 to 1897 he was professor in a secondary school in Budapest and he obtained his habilitation in the university of Budapest. In 1897 he was appointed professor of [[geometry]] in the [[Franz Joseph University|University of Kolozsvár]].{{sfn | Kántor-Varga | 2006 | p=584 }} He retired in 1917 and moved back to Budapest.

He died in 1944 or 1945 in strange circumstances: in the middle of [[World War II]] and aged 91 years, he walked out of his home in [[Budapest]] and he never came back. Likely a victim of racial hate because he was of Jewish descent.{{sfn | Oláh-Gál | 2009 | p=1 }}

His work was greatly influenced by [[Gyula Kőnig]]. His areas of research were [[descriptive geometry]] and [[synthetic geometry]].{{sfn | Kántor-Varga | 2006 | p=585 }} During his retirement in Budapest he encouraged the young [[Edward Teller]] (the father of the [[hydrogen bomb]]).
